1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# scripts/lib/proc-group.sh — process-group resolution and kill helpers.
3	# Extracted from core/router/route.sh (Wave 15-G, #687) so the test stage and
4	# any other long-running spawn share one implementation (#1748).
5	# Sourced library: no set -euo pipefail.
6	
7	[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
8	_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED=1
9	
10	# #2056: there is no setsid prefix any more. Process groups come from `set -m`
11	# at the spawn site — bash job control makes a backgrounded job a group leader,
12	# which is POSIX and identical on macOS and Linux.
13	#
14	# `setsid -w` was wrong here twice over. It is absent on macOS (util-linux is
15	# keg-only), so the prefix went empty, no group was created, and an abort
16	# degraded to a single-PID kill while every descendant survived — the Wave 15-G
17	# guarantee held on Linux only, and the test covering it is Linux-only too, so
18	# nothing said so. And `-w` forces setsid to fork, because it waits for the
19	# child and returns its exit status, so the pid the caller captured was the
20	# wrapper rather than the new session leader.
21	#
22	# Do not reintroduce a prefix here. A spawn that needs an external binary to get
23	# a process group is a spawn whose guarantee is platform-conditional.
24	
25	# Prints the PGID safe to signal for <pid>, or nothing. Empty is not "no group":
26	# it means the group could not be proven distinct from ours, and signalling it
27	# would take down the runner itself — so callers must fall back to a PID kill.
28	zbuild_pg_resolve() {
29	    local _pid="${1:-}"
30	    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
31	    local _child _self
32	    _child="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
33	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
34	    if [[ -n "$_child" && -n "$_self" && "$_child" != "$_self" ]]; then
35	        printf '%s' "$_child"
36	        return 0
37	    fi
38	    # A short-lived child can exit before `ps` reports it. Under `set -m` the
39	    # spawn IS the group leader, so PGID == PID by construction and that stays
40	    # true after it is gone — reporting the pid is correct, not a guess.
41	    #
42	    # This branch previously justified itself with "setsid execs in place, so it
43	    # needs no fork". That was false under `-w` (#2056): setsid forks in order to
44	    # wait, so the captured pid was the wrapper and the group belonged to a
45	    # process one fork below. Under job control there is no wrapper to be wrong
46	    # about.
47	    if [[ -z "$_child" ]]; then
48	        printf '%s' "$_pid"
49	    fi
50	}
51	
52	# TERM <target>, then KILL whatever is left after <grace_s>. Shared by the group
53	# and single-PID paths so both get the same grace — the escalation is the whole
54	# contract, and a caller that skips it is indistinguishable from a plain KILL.
55	#
56	# Synchronous by construction (#905): the `{ sleep 1 && kill -KILL; } &` backstop
57	# this replaces could outlive the caller that armed it, so teardown returned
58	# while the tree was still alive and the backstop was sometimes lost with it.
59	# Polling instead costs milliseconds when the target exits on TERM, costs the
60	# full grace only when it ignores TERM, and leaves nothing running on return.
61	_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill() {
62	    # `--` because a group target is spelled `-PGID` and would otherwise parse
63	    # as an option.
64	    local _target="$1" _grace="$2"
65	    kill -TERM -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
66	    local _ticks=$(( _grace * 10 )) _i=0
67	    while (( _i < _ticks )); do
68	        kill -0 -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || return 0
69	        sleep 0.1 2>/dev/null || true
70	        _i=$(( _i + 1 ))
71	    done
72	    kill -KILL -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
73	}
74	
75	# A non-numeric grace would evaluate to 0 in the arithmetic context above, so the
76	# poll loop would never run and the target would go straight to KILL — silently
77	# losing the escalation the caller asked for. Clamp to the default instead.
78	_zbuild_pg_grace() {
79	    local _g="${1:-1}"
80	    [[ "$_g" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$_g" -gt 0 ]] && printf '%s' "$_g" || printf '1'
81	}
82	
83	# zbuild_pg_record_pgid <file> — the pgid out of a `.pgid` record.
84	#
85	# ONE reader, because there are two formats on disk and three places that read
86	# them (#2018). The engine's dispatch record is `<pgid>\t<leader start time>`;
87	# tool/test's own `test-stage.pgid` is a bare number; and a record written before
88	# #2018 is bare too. A reader that only understands one of those does not error —
89	# it fails the numeric guard and `continue`s, so the caller kills NOTHING and
90	# reports success. That is how a format change here silently disables ADR-062 §2
91	# reclamation, which is the path that actually runs on every normal exit.
92	#
93	# Prints nothing and returns 1 when there is no usable pgid, so a caller can
94	# still distinguish "no record" from "record says 1234".
95	zbuild_pg_record_pgid() {
96	    local _f="${1:-}" _pgid=""
97	    [[ -n "$_f" && -f "$_f" ]] || return 1
98	    IFS=$'\t' read -r _pgid _ 2>/dev/null < "$_f" || true
99	    [[ "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 1
100	    printf '%s' "$_pgid"
101	}
102	
103	# zbuild_pg_register <pgid> — record a process group the caller just created.
104	#
105	# ADR-062 §1 had the ENGINE record this at dispatch. It could not, and the reason
106	# is structural: a stage is a bash function call, not a subprocess, so at the
107	# dispatch seam no group exists yet. That code fell back to `$$`'s group — the
108	# engine's own — which teardown then skipped, correctly, because signalling your
109	# own group takes the runner down with it. Every record was unkillable, every
110	# record was skipped, and §2's kill loop never freed anything (#2024).
111	#
112	# So the direction reverses: whoever CREATES a group registers it. Two sites do,
113	# and only two — `tool/test`'s `set -m` suite and the router's `setsid` spawn.
114	#
115	# Refusing to register our own group is the invariant, not a safety check. A
116	# record naming the registrar's own group is strictly worse than no record: it
117	# cannot be acted on, and it makes the mechanism look live while it does nothing
118	# — which is exactly how the original defect survived #2001, #2018 and an ADR.
119	#
120	# Fail-open throughout: a spawn is never refused because bookkeeping was
121	# unavailable. Silence here costs a possible leak; failing here costs the run.
122	zbuild_pg_register() {
123	    local _pgid="${1:-}"
124	    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
125	    local _self
126	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
127	    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
128	    local _sd="${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}"
129	    [[ -n "$_sd" && -d "$_sd" ]] || return 0
130	    local _stage="${2:-${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}}"
131	    [[ -n "$_stage" ]] || return 0
132	    # One path component, sanitised the same way stage scratch keys are, so no
133	    # stage name can climb out of runtime/.
134	    _stage="${_stage//[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/_}"
135	    local _dir="${_sd}/runtime/stages"
136	    mkdir -p "$_dir" 2>/dev/null || return 0
137	    # #2018 format: the leader's start time proves the pgid still names what
138	    # recorded it, so a later sweep cannot signal a recycled pid.
139	    local _start
140	    _start="$(ps -o lstart= -p "$_pgid" 2>/dev/null | tr -s ' ' | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' || true)"
141	    printf '%s\t%s' "$_pgid" "$_start" > "${_dir}/${_stage}.pgid" 2>/dev/null || true
142	    return 0
143	}
144	
145	# TERM then KILL a whole process group. `-PGID` is the negative-pid convention.
146	zbuild_pg_kill() {
147	    local _pgid="${1:-}"
148	    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
149	    # Refuse our own group: `kill -- -PGID` from inside it takes down the runner.
150	    local _self
151	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
152	    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
153	    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "-$_pgid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
154	}
155	
156	# TERM then KILL a single PID — the path taken when no group could be proven.
157	# It gets the same grace as the group path: a suite that flushes coverage or
158	# writes partial results on SIGTERM needs the window wherever it is killed from.
159	zbuild_pid_kill() {
160	    local _pid="${1:-}"
161	    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
162	    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "$_pid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
163	}

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# core/pipeline/disposition.sh — the disposition vocabulary and the engine's
3	# response table (issue #1822, ADR-054 §6).
4	#
5	# ONE question — "is this failure recoverable?" — answered ONCE, here, from a
6	# field the stage declared. Before this file, four stages answered it four ways:
7	# build's `did_not_finish` carve-out (#1208), design's separate copy of it
8	# (#1261), plan's hand-rolled `return 1` that killed the whole run, and test's
9	# nothing-at-all (#1747). Every new stage added a fifth answer.
10	#
11	# `disposition` is a CLOSED set owned by the engine. #2187 (ADR-054 §6 amended):
12	# each word names a CAUSE a reader must be able to tell apart; many words share
13	# one ACTION. The word never carries a retry count — the template's per-stage
14	# `retry:` budget does:
15	#
16	#   complete       the stage ran; its verdict says how it went      → proceed
17	#   unusable       it ran, but its output cannot be used           → retry
18	#   timed_out      it ran out of time                              → retry
19	#   out_of_turns   it ran out of turn budget                       → retry
20	#   interrupted    an outside signal stopped it                    → retry
21	#   throttled      a short rate limit, recovering                  → wait, retry
22	#   rate_limited   the account's usage limit                       → end run, resumable
23	#   unavailable    an external service zBuild depends on is not    → end run, resumable
24	#                  responding (model provider, GitHub, git remote)
25	#   misconfigured  the setup is wrong (operator fixes it)          → halt
26	#   broken         a defect in zBuild (file a bug)                 → halt
27	#
28	#   (`exhausted` was retired by #2187: it mapped to `escalate`, which nothing
29	#   implemented, and it hid WHICH budget ran out — timed_out / out_of_turns say.)
30	#
31	# The response table lives HERE, not in any plugin: no stage decides its own
32	# retry policy. A stage declares what happened; the engine decides what to do.
33	#
34	# Two rules the rest of the engine depends on:
35	#   - A disposition outside the set is a STRUCTURAL FAILURE. No default is ever
36	#     invented. Inventing one is how "unrecognized is never a failure" — the
37	#     #1819 generator defect — grows back.
38	#   - `broken` is the engine's OWN conclusion about a dispatch that explained
39	#     nothing. The engine never writes it into the stage's artifact; it holds it
40	#     on its own channels (`runner_read_stage_disposition`, the dispatch event).
41	#
42	# NOT in this file, deliberately: the re-dispatch mechanism. ADR-054's delivery
43	# map gives #1822 the vocabulary and the table; nothing owns the loop yet, and
44	# no plugin emits a v2 result to drive one (`grep result_contract plugins/` is
45	# empty). `disposition_retryable` / `disposition_wait_s` state the policy so the
46	# loop, when it lands, reads it instead of re-deriving it.
47	#
48	# Name collision, for the record: ADR-021's member-disposition contract already
49	# writes `.disposition` on plugin primaries with an unrelated vocabulary
50	# (terminal|recoverable|advisory|none — see `_cycle_member_terminal_failure` in
51	# cycle-orchestrator.sh). The two axes are genuinely different: ADR-021 asks
52	# "this stage's verdict was fail — does that stop the cycle?", ADR-054 asks "did
53	# the stage get far enough to produce a verdict worth reading?". They chain; they
54	# do not overlap. #2161: the collision stopped being inert when the acceptance
55	# gate declared `result_contract: 2` — its first fully green run was refused by
56	# this reader. The ADR-021 word now lives in `severity`; `disposition` is this
57	# set only. Readers of the policy word fall back to `disposition` for v1-shaped
58	# results.
59	
60	[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_SH_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
61	_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_SH_LOADED=1
62	
63	# The closed set, in ADR-054 §6 table order.
64	_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_SET="complete unusable timed_out out_of_turns interrupted throttled rate_limited unavailable misconfigured broken"
65	
66	# How long a `throttled` stage waits before a retry. Overridable because the
67	# right backoff is a deployment property, not a contract property; bounded and
68	# validated because it arrives from the environment.
69	_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_THROTTLE_WAIT_DEFAULT=30
70	
71	# ─── disposition_vocabulary ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
72	# The closed set, space-separated, in table order. Callers iterate this rather
73	# than restating the words — a second copy of the list is a second contract.
74	disposition_vocabulary() {
75	    printf '%s' "$_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_SET"
76	}
77	
78	# ─── disposition_is_valid <disposition> ─────────────────────────────────────
79	# rc 0 when the word is a member of the closed set, 1 otherwise. An empty
80	# string is NOT a member: a v1 result declares no disposition at all, and that
81	# absence is distinct from any of the six words.
82	disposition_is_valid() {
83	    local d="${1-}"
84	    [[ -n "$d" ]] || return 1
85	    case " $_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_SET " in
86	        *" $d "*) return 0 ;;
87	        *)        return 1 ;;
88	    esac
89	}
90	
91	# ─── disposition_response <disposition> ─────────────────────────────────────
92	# THE response table. Prints the engine's response and returns 0 for a member of
93	# the set; prints nothing and returns 1 for anything else.
94	#
95	# Refusing to answer for an unknown word is the point: a caller that wants a
96	# response for `wedged` has already failed structurally, and handing it back a
97	# plausible-looking default would bury that.
98	#
99	# `unavailable` and `broken` both stop the run but are NOT interchangeable — an
100	# operator reading the log has to distinguish "something outside us is down, a
101	# human needs to act" from "this is our own defect". They differ in what is
102	# reported, not in the stopping.
103	disposition_response() {
104	    case "${1-}" in
105	        complete)                         printf 'proceed' ;;
106	        unusable|timed_out|out_of_turns)  printf 'retry' ;;
107	        interrupted)                      printf 'retry' ;;
108	        throttled)                        printf 'retry_after_wait' ;;
109	        rate_limited|unavailable)         printf 'halt_unavailable' ;;
110	        misconfigured)                    printf 'halt_misconfigured' ;;
111	        broken)                           printf 'halt_broken' ;;
112	        *)                                return 1 ;;
113	    esac
114	}
115	
116	# ─── disposition_halts <disposition> ────────────────────────────────────────
117	# rc 0 when the engine must stop the run. Derived from the response table rather
118	# than restating it, so the two can never disagree.
119	# A non-member HALTS (#1850, ADR-054 §4 — it was a third rc, 2): an unknown word
120	# is a structural failure, so the one safe answer is to stop.
121	disposition_halts() {
122	    local r; r="$(disposition_response "${1-}")" || return 0
123	    case "$r" in
124	        halt_*) return 0 ;;
125	        *)      return 1 ;;
126	    esac
127	}
128	
129	# ─── disposition_retryable <disposition> ────────────────────────────────────
130	# rc 0 when the engine may re-dispatch the stage. Retry is a property of the
131	# DISPOSITION, not of the stage — this is the inversion ADR-054 §6 describes.
132	# Derived from the response table, which is what makes "nothing both halts and
133	# retries" structurally true rather than a rule someone has to remember.
134	# A non-member is not retryable: it halts (see disposition_halts), and nothing
135	# both halts and retries.
136	disposition_retryable() {
137	    local r; r="$(disposition_response "${1-}")" || return 1
138	    case "$r" in
139	        retry|retry_after_wait) return 0 ;;
140	        *)                      return 1 ;;
141	    esac
142	}
143	
144	# ─── disposition_unfinished <disposition> (#2187) ──────────────────────────
145	# rc 0 when the word says the stage stopped before finishing its work — out of
146	# time, out of turns, or stopped by an outside signal. The cycle reads this, not
147	# a specific word, when it asks "did this iteration finish?".
148	disposition_unfinished() {
149	    case "${1-}" in
150	        timed_out|out_of_turns|interrupted) return 0 ;;
151	        *)                                  return 1 ;;
152	    esac
153	}
154	
155	# ─── disposition_wait_s <disposition> ───────────────────────────────────────
156	# Seconds to wait before re-dispatching. What separates `interrupted` from
157	# `throttled` is not the word but this number: a throttled stage re-dispatched
158	# immediately is simply throttled again, which is a retry loop that burns budget
159	# to learn nothing. Non-members return 1 and print nothing.
160	disposition_wait_s() {
161	    local d="${1-}"
162	    disposition_is_valid "$d" || return 1
163	    # A wait is meaningless for a disposition that is not going to be retried,
164	    # and answering "0" for one is actively dangerous: a caller that skipped
165	    # `disposition_retryable` would read "0 seconds until retry" for `broken`
166	    # and re-dispatch a halted stage immediately. Refuse instead of returning a
167	    # plausible-looking number.
168	    disposition_retryable "$d" || return 1
169	    if [[ "$d" != "throttled" ]]; then
170	        printf '0'
171	        return 0
172	    fi
173	    local w="${ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_THROTTLE_WAIT_S:-$_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_THROTTLE_WAIT_DEFAULT}"
174	    # Environment input: must be a positive integer within a sane bound, else
175	    # fall back to the default rather than honouring a value that would hang a
176	    # run or defeat the wait entirely.
177	    if [[ "$w" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && [[ "$w" -ge 1 ]] && [[ "$w" -le 3600 ]]; then
178	        printf '%s' "$w"
179	    else
180	        printf '%s' "$_ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_THROTTLE_WAIT_DEFAULT"
181	    fi
182	}

1	# ADR-056: run+cleanup-only plugin lifecycle
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Issue:** #1828
5	**Date:** 2026-08-09
6	
7	## Context
8	
9	ADR-001 defined four lifecycle hooks for plugins: `init`, `run`, `finalize`, and `cleanup`.
10	In practice the engine never dispatches `init` or `finalize` — every call site in
11	`runner.sh` and `strategies/common.sh` passes `"run"` to `plugin_hook_call`. The hooks
12	existed in ~30 manifests and ~30 `plugin.sh` files as dead weight: they inflated the
13	contract surface, misled plugin authors, and produced events (`plugin.init.*`,
14	`plugin.finalize.*`) only through test-only direct calls that the live path never emits.
15	
16	A second defect: `plugin_hook_call` returned `0` for an absent optional hook, making an
17	undeclared `cleanup` indistinguishable from one that ran and succeeded — callers could
18	not know whether to escalate or skip.
19	
20	## Decision
21	
22	### 1. Delete `init` and `finalize`
23	
24	Strip `init:` and `finalize:` from every plugin manifest, remove the corresponding
25	functions from every `plugin.sh`, delete the six `plugin.init.*` and `plugin.finalize.*`
26	event types from `config/event-schema.json`, and drop them from
27	`_ZBUILD_YAML_PREWARM_KEYS`. All docs and tests that reference them are updated.
28	
29	### 2. Enforce `run` at registration time with a named failure
30	
31	`validate_manifest` already rejected a missing `run` hook for agent/tool/orchestrator
32	kinds, but the error message was generic. The message now names the specific plugin and
33	hook so failures are immediately actionable:
34	
35	```
36	validate_manifest: plugin 'my-plugin' (kind: agent) requires hook 'run'
37	(declare under hooks: in the manifest)
38	```
39	
40	### 3. Record an absent optional hook on the event stream
41	
42	> **Amended 2026-08-11 (#1823, ADR-054 §4).** As accepted, this section returned exit
43	> code `3` (`ZBUILD_HOOK_ABSENT=3`) for an absent `cleanup`, justified on the grounds
44	> that "the sentinel does not collide with plugin exit-code semantics (0=ok,
45	> 1=recoverable, 2=fatal)" — the ADR-001 rc table that **ADR-054 §4 supersedes**. rc is
46	> binary everywhere, so the sentinel is removed. The requirement it served is unchanged
47	> and still met; only the channel changes.
48	
49	When `plugin_hook_call` is called with `cleanup` and `hooks.cleanup` is absent from the
50	manifest, emit `plugin.cleanup.absent` and return `0`. The absence is visible in the
51	event stream, which is where a consumer that needs to tell "skipped" from "ran cleanly"
52	reads it.
53	
54	Two channels carrying one fact is the defect ADR-054 exists to end, and between the
55	two, the rc is the one nothing can enforce — no engine code ever compared against the
56	`3`. The event was always the load-bearing half: #1828's acceptance asked that an absent
57	hook be "distinguishable in the engine's **records** from a hook that ran and returned
58	0", and the event satisfies that on its own.
59	
60	Consumers: #1829 (teardown dispatch) and #1830 (the teardown stage) read
61	`plugin.cleanup.absent`. Neither issue asks for an exit code — both state the
62	requirement as recording the absence.
63	
64	## Lifecycle after this ADR
65	
66	| Hook | Required? | Absent behavior |
67	|------|-----------|-----------------|
68	| `run` | Yes (agent, tool, orchestrator) | `plugin.run.refused` emitted; rc=1 |
69	| `cleanup` | No (all kinds) | `plugin.cleanup.absent` emitted; rc=0 (amended #1823) |
70	
71	`init` and `finalize` no longer exist in the contract.
72	
73	## Resume contract
74	
75	The `init` hook previously reconstructed state on resume. That responsibility moves into
76	the `run` hook's preamble: plugins that need to recover state on resume check
77	`ZBUILD_RESUMING=1` at the top of their `run` function and read from `state_file`.
78	See `docs/RESUME-CONTRACT.md` for the updated pattern.
79	
80	## Consequences
81	
82	- Plugin authors implement fewer hooks (run + optional cleanup).
83	- Orchestrators distinguish "cleanup skipped" from "cleanup ran cleanly" by reading
84	  `plugin.cleanup.absent`. (As accepted this said the rc=3 sentinel let them do it
85	  "without parsing events"; #1823 removed the sentinel — see the amendment in §3.)
86	- All six `plugin.{init,finalize}.{start,complete,error}` event types are removed from
87	  the schema; any downstream consumer that filtered on them receives nothing.
88	- Tests that called `_init` / `_finalize` functions directly are removed.
89	
90	## Implementation Notes (Phase 0/D1 — issue #1828)
91	
92	- `core/plugin-registry/lifecycle.sh` — `plugin_hook_call` branches on the hook name
93	  when `hooks.<name>` is undeclared: `cleanup` emits `plugin.cleanup.absent` and returns
94	  0, anything else emits `plugin.<hook>.refused` and returns 1. (As accepted this
95	  returned `ZBUILD_HOOK_ABSENT=3`; the constant was deleted by #1823 — see §3.)
96	- `core/plugin-registry/manifest-validation.sh` — the missing-required-hook error names
97	  the plugin id; `_ZBUILD_YAML_PREWARM_KEYS` drops `hooks.init` / `hooks.finalize`.
98	- `config/event-schema.json` — the six `plugin.{init,finalize}.*` types are gone;
99	  `plugin.cleanup.absent` and `plugin.run.refused` are added.
100	- Guard: `tests/unit/plugin-hook-contract-test.sh` greps every `plugins/**/manifest.yaml`
101	  for `init:` / `finalize:` and fails on any hit, so the pair cannot come back.
102	- The ~20 orphaned `cleanup` implementations are **not** touched here — #E1 gives them a
103	  caller, and deleting them now would delete the thing that issue is about to wire up.
104

1	# ADR-062: The engine reclaims; stages stop declaring cleanup hooks
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted (2026-08-31)
4	**Date:** 2026-08-31
5	**Supersedes:** ADR-054 §7's per-stage `cleanup(scope)` dispatch, and the `plugins/tool/teardown` stage that invokes it
6	**Amends:** ADR-056 (the lifecycle becomes `run` only), ADR-058 §1 (`runtime/` gains the writer its definition already promised)
7	**Related:** ADR-059 (issue-vs-run keying — the path is the keying), ADR-011 (the two stores, which this does not reclaim), ADR-052 (engine-owned run worktree)
8	
9	## Context
10	
11	`cleanup(scope)` was made a per-stage hook because of one claim, stated when the teardown stage was introduced:
12	
13	> `plugin.cleanup(scope)` ← **only the stage knows what it spawned**
14	
15	That claim is false, and one plugin in this repository already disproves it.
16	
17	**`tool/test` records what it spawned to disk, and reclaims from the record.** At dispatch it writes `test-stage.pid` and `test-stage.pgid` into `runtime/`, and its cleanup hook reads those files and calls `zbuild_pg_kill`. The stage does not need to *remember* anything: the process group is on disk, and anyone holding the path can act on it.
18	
19	That is the whole mechanism, implemented once, privately, by the only plugin that needed it.
20	
21	### What the other twenty-one hooks do
22	
23	Nothing. Literally:
24	
25	```bash
26	monitor_stage_cleanup() { return 0; }
27	```
28	
29	Of 22 declared `cleanup:` hooks, **21 are `return 0`**. Six carry a comment explaining why they do not emit an event; the rest are three lines. The contract exists, is declared across 22 manifests, is dispatched by a stage plugin, and does nothing 21 times out of 22.
30	
31	### The bug the hook shape guarantees
32	
33	Teardown iterates stages recorded in `.stage_statuses`, and `_update_stage_status` writes that map only with `complete` or `failed` — **after a stage returns**. A stage killed mid-flight is never recorded, so its cleanup never runs.
34	
35	Measured on `runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh`:
36	
37	| Exit path | cleanup dispatched for |
38	|---|---|
39	| success | `intake build test` |
40	| stage rc≠0 | `intake build` |
41	| SIGINT (rc 130) | `intake build` |
42	| **external SIGTERM** | **`intake` only** |
43	| **external hard kill** | **`intake` only** |
44	
45	On the last two, `build` had demonstrably started — it wrote its own marker — and its cleanup never fired. This is the failure #1748 describes: suites observed alive 15+ minutes after a run exited.
46	
47	**A hook cannot fix this, because a hook needs the stage to still be alive to run it.** A record written at spawn survives the stage's death; a hook does not.
48	
49	## Decision
50	
51	### 1. The engine records the process group at dispatch
52	
53	At the dispatch chokepoint the engine writes the spawned process group to `runs/<run_id>/runtime/stages/<stage_id>.pgid`. This is the writer [ADR-058](ADR-058-engine-write-boundary.md) §1 already promised when it defined `runtime/` as holding "PIDs, process groups, staging paths, engine markers" — the definition existed; nothing wrote to it.
54	
55	`runtime/` sits under the run's area, so per [ADR-059](ADR-059-issue-vs-run-keying.md) §1 the record is reclaimable by path like everything else: a reclaimer deletes a `runs/<id>/` and the scope follows from where it sits.
56	
57	### 2. Reclamation reads the record, not the status map
58	
59	`release` kills every recorded process group and drops locks. It **deletes nothing** — ADR-054 §7's rule is unchanged and load-bearing: a failed run keeps its complete evidence.
60	
61	Because the record is written at spawn rather than at completion, a stage killed mid-flight is reclaimable. That is the entire point, and it is what the status-map approach could not do.
62	
63	### 3. Declared no-op hooks leave the contract; the last real one follows
64	
65	**Now.** The 21 `cleanup:` hooks whose entire body is `return 0` are deleted, along with their manifest declarations. Nothing observable changes, which is the point: they were contract surface with no behaviour behind them, and they made `cleanup` look like a live per-stage responsibility when 21 times out of 22 it was not.
66	
67	**`tool/test` keeps its hook for now, and the reason is worth stating rather than hiding.** Its `release` arm is genuinely superseded by §2 — the engine now kills the process group it used to kill. Its `purge` arm is not: it deletes the staging tree, which is a **path** operation, not a process one, and belongs with `zbuild clean --purge`. Retiring the hook before that move would delete the deletion.
68	
69	**Then.** Once `purge`'s staging-tree deletion is a path operation in `zbuild clean`, the last `cleanup:` declaration, the hook name in the plugin contract, `plugins/tool/teardown`'s per-stage dispatch loop, and the `plugin.cleanup.*` event pair retire together, and the lifecycle becomes `run` only.
70	
71	Splitting it this way keeps §4's ordering intact at every step: nothing is removed before the thing that replaces it exists.
72	
73	### 4. Ordering is not negotiable
74	
75	The engine must reclaim **correctly and demonstrably** before a single hook is removed. Retiring first would delete `tool/test`'s working implementation and leave nothing in its place — the one hook that actually frees something.
76	
77	Concretely: §1 and §2 land and are proven equivalent to today's behaviour *including* the SIGTERM/hard-kill cases that currently free nothing; only then does §3 delete anything.
78	
79	## Consequences
80	
81	- **`tool/test`'s private mechanism becomes the engine's.** Its `test-stage.pgid` write and `_test_kill_staging_pg` reader move to the dispatch seam and apply to every stage.
82	- **21 no-op hooks and their manifest declarations disappear.** Nothing observable changes for them, which is the point: they were contract surface with no behaviour behind it.
83	- **The staging-tree deletion in `test_cleanup(purge)` is not a process concern** and moved to `teardown(purge)` as a path operation (#2024). It needed no plugin knowledge in the end: the staging tree is created through `zbuild_engine_tmpdir`, which under dispatch resolves to `ZBUILD_STAGE_SCRATCH` — `<run>/scratch/<stage>` — so it was already inside an engine-owned area. ADR-054 §7's line does not move: purge deletes `scratch/` and nothing else, so a failed run keeps its complete evidence.
84	- **A SIGKILLed runner still leaves orphans until an operator sweeps.** Dispatch runs from an `EXIT` trap and `SIGKILL` cannot be trapped, so nothing in-process can free those groups. The persisted pgid is what makes a *later* sweep possible, and `zbuild cleanup --pgroups` is that sweep (#2018): it reads the records, proves each pgid still names what recorded it, and frees only the proven ones.
85	
86	  The record therefore carries the group leader's **start time** alongside the pgid. A pgid on its own is a number the kernel reissues once the leader is reaped, so a bare record cannot distinguish a leaked group from a stranger holding the same number — and a sweep that guessed would kill someone else's work. Where identity cannot be proven, the sweep skips and names the record; four of its five outcomes refuse to signal anything. A missed leak costs an idle process the operator can see; a wrong kill costs work, silently.
87	
88	  Both formats are on disk — the engine's record with a start time, `tool/test`'s bare `test-stage.pgid`, and any record written before #2018 — so `zbuild_pg_record_pgid` in `scripts/lib/proc-group.sh` is the single reader. Do not re-parse a `.pgid` in a caller: the guard that rejects an unexpected format is a `continue`, so a second parser does not fail loudly, it kills nothing and reports success.
89	- **Reclamation stays bounded.** `ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT` (default 30s) still applies; an unbounded reclaim turns Ctrl-C into a hang, which is the failure the bound exists for.
90	- **Writes outside the data root remain unreclaimable** (#2004). Path-based reclamation cannot reach `${TMPDIR}`; that is fixed by putting writes in bounds, not here.
91	
92	## Implementation Notes
93	
94	The pattern to hoist, from `plugins/tool/test/plugin.sh`:
95	
96	```bash
97	_runtime_dir="$(_test_runtime_dir "$(dirname "$(dirname "$output_json")")")"
98	printf '%s' "$tmp" > "$_runtime_dir/test-staging-path"
99	# writes test-stage.pid and test-stage.pgid, then:
100	trap "_test_kill_staging_pg '$_pid_file' '$_pgid_file'" RETURN
101	```
102	
103	and its reader, which is already generic:
104	
105	```bash
106	_test_kill_staging_pg() {
107	    _pgid="$(cat "$_gf")" ; zbuild_pg_kill "$_pgid"
108	}
109	```
110	
111	`zbuild_pg_kill` and `_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill` (`scripts/lib/proc-group.sh`) are the existing kill mechanism and need no change — only a caller that reads from disk rather than from a shell variable. `zbuild_pg_resolve` already derives a child's pgid at spawn time; today the result lives in a shell variable and dies with the process (`core/router/route.sh`, `core/pipeline/runner.sh:2159-2194`).
112	
113	Verification:
114	
115	```bash
116	bash tests/integration/runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh   # SPEC-4/5 must free build, not just intake
117	bash tests/unit/core-pipeline-lifecycle-test.sh
118	npm run test:unit && npm test && npm run lint
119	```
120	
121	The discriminating case is the external hard kill: today it frees `intake` only. If it still frees `intake` only after §1 and §2, the record is not being written at spawn and nothing else in this ADR works.
122	
123	**That test was never run, and §1 as originally written could not have passed it (#2024).** The record was taken at the dispatch seam from `$$` — but a stage is a bash function call, not a subprocess, so no group exists there and `$$` names the *engine's own* group. teardown skipped every record, correctly, because signalling your own group takes the runner down. §2's kill loop freed nothing, and the number on disk looked entirely plausible.
124	
125	The correction reverses the direction: the engine cannot observe a group that does not exist yet, so **whoever creates one registers it** — `zbuild_pg_register` (`scripts/lib/proc-group.sh`), called from the two sites that make groups, `tool/test`'s `set -m` suite and the router's `setsid` spawn. Registering your own group is refused, because that is precisely the unkillable record. The dispatch-time write is deleted rather than fixed: any pgid observable at that seam is by definition one that cannot be signalled from inside the run.
126	
127	§4's ordering held up exactly as written. `tool/test`'s hook was the only mechanism in the tree that had ever killed a stage's children; retiring it before the engine worked would have removed the one thing that functioned and replaced it with one that never had.
128	
129	`tests/integration/hard-kill-sweep-e2e-test.sh` is the discriminating test, and it is now real: it SIGKILLs the runner, confirms the suite outlives it, and asserts the next sweep frees it. It does not skip when it cannot stage the scenario — a skip here is indistinguishable from the mechanism being broken.

## Search Results and Findings

I've completed a thorough analysis of the zBuild codebase for your design task. Here are the full contents and findings:

### Files Read

**1. `/core/pipeline/runner.sh`** (3976 lines, partial read shown)
The main pipeline orchestrator. Key findings:
- Lines 152-166: `_runner_retry_budget()` — manages stage retry limits based on template config, environment, or engine defaults (capped at 5)
- Lines 2372-2490: Timeout/watchdog handling for always-run stages with `ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT` (default 30s), using `set -m` for job control
- Lines 2414-2444: `_runner_dispatch_always_run()` dispatches stages that run on every exit path
- The runner uses process group signaling via `zbuild_pg_kill` from `scripts/lib/proc-group.sh`
- Disposition vocabulary is consulted via `runner_read_stage_disposition()` (line 2976)

**2. `/core/pipeline/template.sh`** (2789 lines, partial read shown)
Template loading and stage resolution. Key aspects:
- Manages both old and new template shapes
- Parses cycle entries, parallel groups, and map groups
- Stores per-stage attributes in `_TPL_STAGE_*` variables
- Stage membership validation via `_runner_validate_leaf_resolvability()`
- Disposition vocabulary is declared but read elsewhere

**3. `/scripts/lib/stage-limits.sh`** (162 lines, complete)
Per-stage router configuration. Key functions:
- `_route_resolve_knob()` — implements precedence: template > env > manifest > constant
- `_route_resolve_timeout()` — resolves per-stage router timeout (default 300s)
- `_route_resolve_max_turns()` — resolves max turns budget (default 25)
- `_route_resolve_max_iterations()` — resolves max iterations (default 10)
- `_route_resolve_retries()` — resolves retry count on timeout (default 0)

**4. `/scripts/lib/abort-propagation.sh`** (92 lines, complete)
ADR-025 abort propagation contract. Key mechanisms:
- Two-layer abort system: rc-driven + sentinel-file driven (for cross-subshell)
- `_zbuild_abort()` — records abort word (default `sigint`)
- `_zbuild_check_abort()` — returns 1 if abort recorded
- `_zbuild_propagate_abort()` — returns 1 when child failed AND abort recorded
- Sentinel file: `${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR}/.abort.signal` survives env scrubs

**5. `/scripts/lib/proc-group.sh`** (164 lines, complete)
Process group resolution and termination. Key functions:
- `zbuild_pg_resolve()` — derives the PGID safe to signal for a PID
- `zbuild_pg_register()` — records a spawned process group to `runtime/stages/<stage>.pgid`
- `zbuild_pg_kill()` — TERM then KILL a process group (with 1s grace default)
- `zbuild_pid_kill()` — TERM then KILL a single PID when no group available
- Uses synchronous escalation (no detached backstop)

**6. `/docs/adr/ADR-025-abort-propagation.md`** (full, 409 lines)
Abort propagation contract. Critical details:
- Two dispatch-site helpers in every loop: pre-flight `_zbuild_check_abort`, post-flight `_zbuild_propagate_abort`
- Amendment #1850 (2026-10-08): abort is a recorded word, not an rc; helpers return 0 or 1
- Abort words: `sigint`, `sigterm`, `cycle_abort`, `llm_unavailable`, `llm_rate_limited`, `scope_too_large`
- Sentinel file holds the word; first recorded abort wins
- Runner exits with code 1; abort word is in `pipeline.aborted reason=<word>`

**7. `/docs/adr/ADR-054-stage-contract.md`** (full, 464 lines)
Stage contract specification. Critical sections:
- **§4**: Exit codes are binary — rc ∈ {0,1} everywhere
- **§6**: Disposition vocabulary (closed set, engine-owned):
  - `complete`, `unusable`, `timed_out`, `out_of_turns`, `interrupted`, `throttled`, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`, `misconfigured`, `broken`
  - `timed_out` and `out_of_turns` both map to "retry" action
  - `interrupted` is for outside signals, `throttled` is for short rate limits
  - `unavailable` ends run (resumable), `misconfigured`/`broken` halt
- **§7**: Teardown/cleanup is now dispatch-triggered with `release` or `purge` scope
- Amendment #2287 (2026-10-04): always-run stages run under time bounds; timeout TERM's entire process group then KILL

**8. `/config/adr-enforcement-baseline.txt`** (60 lines)
ADRs without "Enforced by" sections yet (list only shrinks as tests added). Notes that ADR-054 has no tests section yet.

### Additional Key Files Found

**`/core/pipeline/disposition.sh`** — The disposition response table and policy functions
- Vocabulary: complete, unusable, timed_out, out_of_turns, interrupted, throttled, rate_limited, unavailable, misconfigured, broken
- `disposition_response()` — maps each word to an action (proceed, retry, retry_after_wait, halt_unavailable, halt_misconfigured, halt_broken)
- `disposition_halts()` — returns 0 when engine must stop the run
- `disposition_retryable()` — returns 0 when stage may be re-dispatched
- `disposition_unfinished()` — returns 0 for `timed_out|out_of_turns|interrupted`
- `disposition_wait_s()` — seconds to wait before retry (30s default for throttled)

### Search Results Summary

**Functions where `zbuild_pg_kill` is used:**
- `/plugins/tool/teardown/plugin.sh` — calls `zbuild_pg_kill` to kill recorded process groups
- `/plugins/tool/test/plugin.sh` — calls `zbuild_pg_kill` from cleanup
- `/scripts/lib/cleanup.sh` — sweeps and kills recorded process groups
- `/core/router/route.sh` — uses process group killing for route loop abort

**Timeout/Timed-Out References:**
- Router timeout (rc=124) → `disposition=timed_out` (not router_timeout as event reason)
- Out-of-turns timeout (turn budget exhausted) → `disposition=out_of_turns`
- Both retry under template's per-stage `retry:` budget or `ZBUILD_DISPOSITION_REDISPATCH`
- No `max_run_s` or `ZBUILD_MAX_RUN_S` in codebase — per-stage timeouts only

**Disposition References in Core:**
- `/core/pipeline/verdict.sh` — reads stage result files
- `/core/pipeline/dispatch-rc.sh` — maps rc to disposition
- `/core/pipeline/runner.sh` — reads disposition and acts on it
- `/core/pipeline/cycle-orchestrator.sh` — disposition-driven member retry logic

**No Tests Named:**
- `*run-limit*`, `*run-timed-out*`, `*watchdog*`, `*resume-after-run*` not found
- Actual tests: `runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh`, `hard-kill-sweep-e2e-test.sh`, `test-stage-proc-group-test.sh`

### Architecture Summary for Your Design

**Current State:**
- Stage dispatch happens with `set -m` (bash job control) to create process groups
- Process groups are recorded at spawn time via `zbuild_pg_register()` to `runtime/stages/<stage>.pgid`
- Timeout handling: per-stage `router.timeout_s` (default 300s) in router, not engine
- Always-run stages (release/persist) get their own time bounds via `ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT` (default 30s)
- On timeout: router returns rc=124, which maps to `disposition=timed_out`, which retries (if budget remains)
- Abort propagation: words recorded once (not rcs) in process and on disk; first wins; helpers at pre/post-flight

**Key Design Patterns:**
1. **Disposition** is the declared field for recoverability (not inferred from verdict)
2. **Process groups** are the unit of cleanup (not individual PIDs)
3. **Records on disk** survive process death (sentinel files, pgid files)
4. **Time bounds** apply to always-run stages via watchdog process group signaling
5. **Retry budgets** come from template config, environment, or engine defaults (capped)

This gives you the foundation for designing run-level timeout management and process lifecycle handling in zBuild.

46	# compile-time constant is the floor:

_route_classify_max_turns_source() {

    else

    # #612: SIGINT marker — set by the INT trap so the EXIT trap can record
    # `pipeline.aborted reason=sigint` durably (the trap itself runs in the
    # signal handler context; we centralize the state/event writes in EXIT).
    # Wave 15-F (#686): _RUNNER_ABORT_REASON records which signal fired
    # (sigint|sigterm) so the EXIT trap can emit reason=sigint vs reason=sigterm.
    # _RUNNER_SIGINT_RECEIVED is preserved (set on either signal) for backward
    # compatibility with any consumer keying off the legacy marker.
    _RUNNER_SIGINT_RECEIVED=0
    _RUNNER_ABORT_REASON=""

    # Wave 15-H (#688): flag-gated bash job-control + process-group signal
    # forwarding. Default OFF — flag-off behavior is byte-identical to today.
    # When ZBUILD_RUNNER_JOB_CONTROL=1:
    #   - `set -m` enables job control so every backgrounded child gets its
    #     own PGID equal to its PID;
    #   - the SIGINT/TERM trap walks `jobs -p` and TERM-then-KILL's each
    #     PGID, reaping whole subtrees (not just direct PIDs).
    # This is belt-and-suspenders to the existing per-site kills:
    #   - Wave 8 (#612) per-PID kill in the build plugin,
    #   - Wave 15-G (#687) PG-kill in the router around `setsid -w` claude.
    # Both stay as fallback; Wave 15-H adds wider coverage for any future
    # backgrounded children of the runner shell. Safety considerations:
    #   - `jobs -p` is empty when no backgrounded children exist → trap loop
    #     is a safe no-op (no spurious kills).
    #   - `set -m` makes bash auto-disown completed children; the existing
    #     synchronous foreground dispatch path (plugin_hook_call subshells)
    #     is unaffected because `wait` semantics on direct foreground
    #     children are preserved.
    #   - The runner's own PGID becomes its session leader's PGID; the
    #     test harness's kernel-pgrp delivery still reaches it.
    if [[ "${ZBUILD_RUNNER_JOB_CONTROL:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
        set -m
    fi

    # ── ADR-054 §7 (#1829) / #1831: always-run stages on EVERY exit path ─────
    # Success, non-zero rc, SIGINT, SIGTERM and timeout all funnel through the
    # EXIT trap below, which is why the dispatch lives there and not at the end
    # of main() — an exit path that skipped it would leak whatever the stage
    # spawned. #1759 is the prerequisite: without re-armed INT/TERM traps there
    # is no signal path for this to hang off.
    #
    # #1831: WHICH stages run here is the TEMPLATE's decision, not the engine's.
    # This used to name one plugin by directory (`plugins/tool/teardown`) and
    # degrade to a no-op if it was absent — the engine knowing one plugin's path
    # is the coupling ADR-047 forbids, and a silent no-op is how #1878's sibling
    # mechanism went uninvoked without anything noticing. The list now comes
    # from the template's `always_run:`, resolved by role through the same
    # `resolve_plugin_for_role` seam every dispatch strategy uses.
    #
    # Scope stays pinned to `release` for the teardown role: free live resources
    # and delete NOTHING, so a failed run keeps all of its evidence on disk.
    # `purge` is operator-only and unreachable from any run path.
    _runner_dispatch_always_run() {
        [[ -n "${_runner_state_file:-}" && -f "${_runner_state_file}" ]] || return 0
        [[ "${#_TPL_ALWAYS_RUN[@]}" -gt 0 ]] || return 0
        local plugins_root="${ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT:-$_ZBUILD_ROOT/plugins}"
        local _ar_stage _ar_safe _ar_role _ar_to _ar_dir _ar_guard
        for _ar_stage in "${_TPL_ALWAYS_RUN[@]}"; do
            _ar_safe="${_ar_stage//-/_}"
            # Per-stage, not global: the trap can be reached more than once, and
            # there is now more than one always-run stage to keep track of.
            _ar_guard="_RUNNER_AR_DISPATCHED_${_ar_safe}"
            [[ "${!_ar_guard:-0}" == "1" ]] && continue
            printf -v "$_ar_guard" '%s' 1

            local _ar_roles_var="_TPL_STAGE_ROLES_${_ar_safe}"
            _ar_role="${!_ar_roles_var:-}"
            [[ -n "$_ar_role" ]] || continue
            # roles: is a list; an always-run stage takes the first.
            _ar_role="${_ar_role%%,*}"

            _ar_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$_ar_role" "" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            if [[ -z "$_ar_dir" || ! -d "$_ar_dir" ]]; then
                # LOUD, unlike the old `[[ -d ... ]] || return 0`. An always-run
                # stage that cannot be resolved has not run, and the operator
                # needs to know that rather than infer it from a missing effect.
                eb_emit_event "stage.always_run.unresolved" "stage=$_ar_stage" "role=$_ar_role" 2>/dev/null || true
                continue
            fi

            local _ar_to_var="_TPL_STAGE_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_${_ar_safe}"
            _ar_to="${!_ar_to_var:-}"
            [[ "$_ar_to" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$_ar_to" -gt 0 ]] || _ar_to="${ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT:-30}"

            # Bounded, because this runs inside the EXIT trap: a hook that blocks
            # would turn a Ctrl-C into a hang — the exact class of bug this
            # mechanism exists to prevent. A timeout BINARY cannot be used here
            # (plugin_hook_call is a shell function; timeout can only exec a
            # command, so the wrapper would fail with "command not found" and
            # silently skip every dispatch). The bound is therefore a watchdog
            # that is CANCELLED on the normal path, so no stray `sleep` outlives
            # the run.
            #
            # `|| true` because an always-run stage's failure is recorded as an
            # event and must NEVER change the run's exit status.
            #
            # #2287: the bound must stop the hook, not just stop waiting for it.
            # Signalling the one PID reached only the outer shell: the subshell
            # running the stage hooks, and anything it spawned, lived on after
            # the run and wrote into its state minutes later. `set -m` (as the
            # router's model spawn does, #2056) makes each job a process-group
            # leader, so `kill -- -<pid>` reaches the whole tree — TERM, then
            # KILL after a short grace for a hook that traps TERM. The watchdog
            # gets its own group too, so cancelling it leaves no `sleep` behind.
            (
                export ZBUILD_TEARDOWN_SCOPE=release
                set -m
                plugin_hook_call "$_ar_dir" run "$_ar_stage" "$_runner_state_file" &
                _ar_pid=$!
                ( set +m; sleep "$_ar_to"; kill -TERM -- -"$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
                  sleep 2; kill -KILL -- -"$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null || true ) &
                _wd_pid=$!
                set +m
                wait "$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
                # #2333: the leader exiting does not mean its group did. A member
                # that ignored TERM would lose its KILL when the watchdog is
                # cancelled below, so KILL the group now; a no-op when it is gone.
                kill -KILL -- -"$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
                kill -TERM -- -"$_wd_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
                wait "$_wd_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
            ) >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
        done
        return 0
    }

    _runner_abort_trap() {
        # #1829: free live resources first, while the state file and the
        # process tree are still intact.
        _runner_dispatch_always_run
        # #1688: release the issue lock EXPLICITLY. Relying on process death is
        # not enough — a flock belongs to the open file description, which every
        # child inherits, so one lingering child would keep the issue locked
        # after this run is gone. Released after the always-run stages, which
        # still belong to this run.
        if declare -F zbuild_issue_lock_release >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            zbuild_issue_lock_release || true
        fi
        if declare -F zbuild_run_cap_release >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            zbuild_run_cap_release || true
        fi
        # ADR-025 (Wave 15-B #684): the sentinel must be cleared on EVERY
        # exit path — clean end, normal failure, or abort — so a follow-on
        # zbuild invocation in the same state_dir never sees a stale
        # signal. Runs BEFORE the short-circuit because the
        # `_runner_ended=true` path is the common case (every successful
        # run hits it) and that path also needs the cleanup.
        _zbuild_disarm_abort_sentinel
        # Best-effort: drop THIS run's own lock siblings so a killed run does
        # not leave a stale .lock behind. flock releases on fd close at process
        # death regardless, but the on-disk lock FILE would otherwise linger;
        # this is belt-and-suspenders to the authoritative --no-resume startup
        # clear (the trap may be deferred behind a foreground `wait`, #run-hygiene).
        if [[ -n "${_runner_state_file:-}" ]]; then
            local _rd; _rd="$(dirname "$_runner_state_file")"
            rm -f "$_runner_state_file.lock" "$_rd/events.jsonl.lock" \
                  "$_rd/events.db.lock" 2>/dev/null || true
        fi
        # #2131: the normal path — pipeline.end and the always-run stages are
        # on disk; the sidecar renders them in its final PATCH, then goes.
        if [[ "$_runner_ended" == "true" ]]; then _runner_status_comment_reap; return 0; fi
        # Clean teardown (signal/OOM) → interrupted; operator cancel → aborted handled elsewhere.
        # Fail-closed: if we cannot mark the pipeline interrupted, emit an error event so the
        # operator can detect the unrecorded abort (was: || true, which silently dropped failures).
        if ! _set_pipeline_status "$_runner_state_file" "interrupted" 2>/dev/null; then
            eb_emit_event "pipeline.state.error" \
                "run_id=$_runner_run_id" "issue=$_runner_issue" \
                "reason=abort_trap_set_status_failed" 2>/dev/null || true
        fi
        # #612: when the abort was caused by a signal, emit a distinguishable
        # `pipeline.aborted reason=<sigint|sigterm> status=interrupted` event so
        # the operator/postmortem can tell a Ctrl-C / kill from an OOM or fatal
        # stage rc. Always emit the legacy `pipeline.abort` too so existing
        # consumers don't break.
        # Wave 15-F (#686): reason carries the signal name (sigint|sigterm)
        # captured by _runner_signal_trap. Fall back to "sigint" for backward
        # compat if the marker is set but the reason was not recorded (a path
        # that should not occur but is cheap to guard).
        if [[ "${_RUNNER_SIGINT_RECEIVED:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
            eb_emit_event "pipeline.aborted" \
                "run_id=$_runner_run_id" "issue=$_runner_issue" \
                "reason=${_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON:-sigint}" "status=interrupted" 2>/dev/null || true
        fi
        # Fail-closed: if abort event cannot be emitted, that is still non-fatal for the trap
        # itself (the process is exiting), but we do not silently swallow the failure.
        if ! eb_emit_event "pipeline.abort" \
            "run_id=$_runner_run_id" "issue=$_runner_issue" 2>/dev/null; then
            : # trap is exiting anyway; best-effort only
        fi
        # #525: terminal banner for the operator. Event already emitted above
        # so banner-render failure cannot lose the durable record. Reuses the
        # ✗ RED "aborted" rendering path (per ADR-015 §v5 amendment).
        # NB: do NOT redirect stderr away here — the banner writes to fd 2.
        # Wrap in a subshell so a non-zero rc inside doesn't abort the trap.
        ( _render_pipeline_end "aborted" ) || true
        # #2131: abnormal path — pipeline.aborted/pipeline.abort are on disk
        # now, so the sidecar's final render says why. Last, deliberately.
        _runner_status_comment_reap
    }

1	# ADR-054: Stage Contract
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted (2026-08-09)
4	**Date:** 2026-08-09
5	**Issue:** #1820
6	**Amended:** 2026-10-07 (#1798) — §4: a leaf stage whose verdict is fail-class ends the run unless its template marks it `blocking: false` (Amendment at the end).
7	**Amended:** 2026-09-16 (#2111) — §6: a rate limit observed by the router resolves to `unavailable`, not `throttled`. The engine now enforces `halt_unavailable` on the cycle dispatch path (it was announced only): the run ends `aborted` with `reason=llm_rate_limited` and the reset text under `.rate_limit.message`, state persisted for ADR-050 resume. `throttled` stays in the closed set with no rate-limit emitter. Waiting and retrying re-entered the same limit for five iterations on #1840/#1841, re-verifying an unchanged tree each time.
8	**Amended:** 2026-08-23 (#141) — §7: the three-actor table is run-keyed in every row; the **issue** is a second scope, and `release` gains the `always-run` attribute plus a `persist` sibling (ADR-059).
9	**Amended:** 2026-08-23 (#1920) — §7: the `release` "deletes nothing" promise scoped to the run's own lifecycle; operator-invoked reclamation (`zbuild cleanup --state-dirs`) named as a third actor with its own clock and guards.
10	**Amended:** 2026-08-12 (#1862) — §3.1 added: the engine exports dispatch identity (`ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE`, `ZBUILD_PLUGIN`, `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_KIND`, `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR`) at `plugin_hook_call`, scoped to one dispatch. A plugin is self-defining about what it is and can never be self-defining about which stage it serves. `ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT` is explicitly excluded; identity is scrubbed by `env-scrub` per ADR-024, not exempted from it.
11	**Amends:**
12	- ADR-001 — the stage contract is two hooks (§1), rc ∈ {0,1} (§4), and one result file (§5). The rc=1→`kind: recovery` routing is deleted; it was never implemented and no recovery plugin was ever registered.
13	- ADR-021 — verdict and disposition are separated (§6); the informally-inherited `pass|warn|fail|unknown|error|corrupt_diff|block` set, which carried both axes in one string, is replaced.
14	- ADR-025 — the runner still owns the trap, but `cleanup` is no longer an abort-only notification: it is dispatched by a `teardown` stage with a `scope` (§7).
15	- ADR-045 — superseded by the same verdict/disposition split (§6).
16	**Related:** ADR-001 (plugin contract), ADR-013 (canonical stage list), ADR-017 (per-stage router config), ADR-047 (stage-agnostic mechanics — the parent principle this extends), ADR-055 (inter-stage data contract v2), ADR-056 (run+cleanup-only lifecycle)
17	
18	## Context
19	
20	**This ADR is a specification, not a description.** It states the contract Phase 0 (#1819) implements; each section names the issue that delivers it. Where the engine does not yet behave this way, that is recorded as the gap it is — the whole reason for writing it down.
21	
22	ADR-001 defined the general plugin contract for all plugin kinds. The stage-bound subset was never extracted, and the parts of ADR-001 that touched it were aspirational in a way nothing ever reconciled:
23	
24	| ADR-001 said | The engine did |
25	|---|---|
26	| Four hooks: `init`, `run`, `finalize`, `cleanup` | Five `plugin_hook_call` sites, **all `run`**. Three of the four were never called — including `cleanup`, which 20+ plugins nevertheless implement. |
27	| `rc=1` routes to `kind: recovery` plugins; `rc=2` is fatal | **No recovery plugin has ever been registered.** Stages return 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 143. |
28	| `valid_verdicts` declares a plugin's vocabulary | ~~**No engine code reads it.** Adoption: 1 of 25.~~ **Closed by #1708**: adoption is 25 of 25, and `scripts/lib/lint-verdict-classify.sh` fails the build when a declared verdict is not classified. |
29	
30	The pattern is one defect, not three: **a declaration nothing enforces.** An unknown verdict draws a yellow glyph; an undeclared hook returns `0` silently; a zero-byte artifact passes the fail-closed scanner. Unrecognized is never a failure, so the document and the engine were free to drift apart for the life of the project.
31	
32	ADR-054 fixes the call and response surfaces — hooks, arguments, exit codes, the result file, and the verdict/disposition split. ADR-055 fixes the data and declaration surfaces. Together they are the interface Phase 0 enforces.
33	
34	### Why this precedes the rest of Initiative 1.3
35	
36	Initiative 1.3 (#1818) is one defect wearing different clothes across seven phases: the engine and its stages have no enforced interface. Phase 1 (#1794) makes a failing leaf stage stop the run — the single most valuable change in the milestone, and **unshippable without this contract**.
37	
38	Today a router timeout surfaces as `verdict=error`. Make a failing verdict terminal without first separating *what happened* from *what to do about it*, and a network hiccup on `intake` or `impact` becomes a dead run. `interrupted` and `throttled` exist so that the same event can stop a run that is genuinely broken and retry one that merely stalled. That is the whole reason the disposition vocabulary (§6) is a declared field rather than a string the engine re-interprets.
39	
40	The same dependency runs through the rest: Phase 3 cannot enforce declarations that were never load-bearing (ADR-055), Phase 4 cannot safely delete code whose reachability nothing can prove, and Phase 5's acceptance work measures assertions against a result file whose shape this ADR fixes. **Every phase either depends on this contract or is a consequence of not having had one.**
41	
42	## Decision
43	
44	### 1. The call surface: two hooks
45	
46	The contract has exactly **two** hooks:
47	
48	| Hook | Required | Invoked by |
49	|------|----------|------------|
50	| `run` | Yes | Every stage dispatch |
51	| `cleanup` | No | A `teardown` stage, with a `scope` (§7) |
52	
53	`init` and `finalize` are deleted from the contract. ADR-056 (#1828) carries out that deletion and owns the resulting lifecycle — including registration-time enforcement of `run` and the `rc=3` sentinel that distinguishes an absent optional hook from one that ran. This ADR does not restate those rules; it specifies the two surviving hooks' arguments (§2) and `cleanup`'s trigger and scope (§7).
54	
55	**What was true before this contract.** Three of the four hooks ADR-001 documented were never called: there are five `plugin_hook_call` sites in the engine and every one passes `run`. `init` and `finalize` were dead. `cleanup` was also dead — never dispatched by anything — yet **20+ plugins ship one**, written to a documented interface and drifting untested for the life of the project. That is the failure mode this ADR exists to end: a document describing a lifecycle the engine implemented one fifth of, with nothing reconciling the two.
56	
57	### 2. Hook signatures
58	
59	```
60	run(stage_id, state_file, resolved_inputs)
61	cleanup(stage_id, state_file, scope)
62	```
63	
64	- `stage_id` — the dispatching stage's id.
65	- `state_file` — absolute path to `pipeline-state.json`. Plugins derive `state_dir = dirname($2)` and `artifacts_dir = $state_dir/artifacts`.
66	- `resolved_inputs` — the engine resolves every input the manifest declares and hands them over. **A plugin never rebuilds a path.** Delivered by #1826; until then a plugin reads its declared inputs itself.
67	- `scope` — `release` or `purge` (§7).
68	
69	### 3. Runtime environment
70	
71	Run-time context is passed via env vars exported by the runner — never via positional args. The current set for stage-bound hooks:
72	
73	| Env var | Set by | Available to |
74	|---------|--------|--------------|
75	| `ZBUILD_GOAL` | runner | all hooks |
76	| `ZBUILD_ISSUE` | runner | all hooks (empty string when absent) |

86	#### 3.1 Dispatch identity — amended 2026-08-12 (#1862)
87	
88	**The engine states, for exactly the span of one dispatch, which stage this is and which plugin serves it.** The single export point is `plugin_hook_call` (`core/plugin-registry/lifecycle.sh`).
89	
90	| Variable | Value | Source |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| `ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE` | the dispatching stage's name | `stage_id` — `$1` of the hook signature (§2) |
93	| `ZBUILD_PLUGIN` | the serving plugin's `id` | `$plugin_dir/manifest.yaml` |
94	| `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_KIND` | the serving plugin's `kind` | `$plugin_dir/manifest.yaml` |
95	| `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR` | the serving plugin's directory | `$1` of `plugin_hook_call` |
96	| `ZBUILD_UNIT` | this unit's own name: the stage, or `<stage>.<element>` for a map member — `<stage>.<role>.<element>` when the map runs more than one role (amended 2026-10-03, #1706) | `stage_id` plus the element the map generator bakes into the work unit |
97	
98	**Why the engine and not the plugin.** A plugin is self-defining about *what it is* — `scripts/lib/plugin-bootstrap.sh` resolves `_ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR` from the plugin's own `BASH_SOURCE`, needing no engine. It can never be self-defining about *which stage it is currently serving*. Stage name, role and plugin id are three distinct namespaces and only the template holds the mapping: `review_lenses` (stage) is served by `review-lens` (plugin id) via role `review_lens`, and under `map:` all six lens members receive that one stage name. Everything keyed to the flow — the run timeline, `stage_statuses`, the per-stage router knobs — needs the stage name; introspection yields only the plugin id.
99	
100	The engine's answer cannot differ from the plugin's own: `plugin_hook_call` sources `plugin.sh` from the same directory it stamps, and reads `id`/`kind` from the same manifest the plugin would. It is the plugin's answer plus the axis the plugin cannot reach.
101	
102	**Why `plugin_hook_call`.** It is the only site reaching all four dispatch arms. The `map:` arm executes a generated standalone script (`core/pipeline/strategies/common.sh`) that the runner cannot export into — but `plugin_hook_call` is that script's last line.
103	
104	**Lifetime is one dispatch.** Declared `local -x`, not `export`. This reaches the lifecycle's own `plugin.*` emits (which fire outside the plugin subshell), reaches the subshell and anything it spawns, and unsets on return. Identity from stage *N* must not be visible during stage *N+1*; a plain `export` would trade a blank field for a stale one.
105	
106	**Each unit has its own name — amended 2026-10-03 (#1706).** Under `map:` every member receives the group's stage name, and that stays: the group is what template settings (router budgets, retries) are looked up by. But the members run at the same time, so anything a member writes or emits under the stage name alone collides. #2032 run 37066151065 lost red-team's diagnosis this way: the router named its error record `review_lenses-sync-error`, and the correctness lens's record overwrote it. So:
107	
108	- `ZBUILD_UNIT` is `<stage>.<element>` for a map member (the declared element, or the platform for a map over platforms) and the stage name otherwise. It lives for one dispatch, like the rest of this table. A stage dispatched from inside a member is named by its own stage. Enforced by `tests/unit/unit-name-test.sh` U1–U3.
109	- An engine event emitted inside a member carries `unit` in its envelope; an event outside a map carries no `unit` key, so every other envelope is unchanged. Enforced by U4.
110	- Per-member records are named by the unit; the router's error record is the first (`<unit>-sync-error`). Enforced by U5. The router's throttle and turn-budget markers stay keyed by stage, because the runner reads them at the group level, outside the members.
111	- A map that runs more than one role runs every role on every element, so the role is part of the name: `<stage>.<role>.<element>`. Enforced by U7.
112	- **Two units with one name never start together.** A map whose members would share a name is refused before any member starts (rc 1 — failed, per §4; the `strategy.unit_name_conflict` event names the duplicate). Enforced by U6.
113	
114	**Two owners, two questions, deliberately not merged.** `_ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR` (plugin-owned, set at source time) answers *where are my files on disk* and must keep working when a plugin is sourced with no engine present. `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR` (engine-owned, set at dispatch) answers *who is this dispatch for*. In production they are always equal. Plugin code uses the former to locate its own assets; shared engine libraries use the latter to know whom they serve.
115	
116	**`ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT` is not identity and is not set here.** Every reader spells it `${ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT:-<repo default>}` — it is an operator override, and ADR-024 / `scripts/lib/persona-resolve.sh` forbid relying on it as a root. Engine-setting it would convert an override into a permanent pin. Derive from `ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR`.
117	
118	**Identity does not survive `env-scrub`.** Per ADR-024 the claude spawn is a fresh-user-shell subprocess that must not see `ZBUILD_*` pipeline state, and identity is pipeline state. Every consumer — the router's knob resolver, `stage_io_begin`, envelope stamping — runs in the parent scope before the spawn. `_zbuild_make_fresh_shell` scrubs identity along with everything else, and a regression guard asserts it.

120	#### 3.2 Context is not data — added 2026-08-12 (#1768)
121	
122	The variables in §3 and §3.1 are **engine context**: they describe *the invocation*, not *the work*. Everything a stage consumes that describes the work is a **declared input**, resolved by the engine and handed to `run` (ADR-055 §1).
123	
124	| | Examples | How a stage gets it |
125	|---|---|---|
126	| **Context** — describes the invocation | run id, issue number, current stage, plugin identity (§3.1), cycle iteration, map element, target platform, state dir | ambient environment |
127	| **Data** — describes the work | a scope manifest, a plan, a diff, gate results, the issue body, the goal, the working tree | a declared input |
128	
129	The discriminator: **would a different template give this a different value for the same work?** Yes → context. No → data.
130	
131	This line matters because it was not drawn. Exactly one stage declares an external input today while ten plugins read `ZBUILD_ISSUE` straight from the environment — the issue body and the goal are *data*, arriving through the context channel, declared nowhere and checkable by nothing. ADR-055 §1.2 moves them; the variables above stay where they are.

133	### 4. Exit codes (rc)
134	
135	Exit codes are **binary — everywhere, not only at the plugin boundary**:
136	
137	| rc | Meaning |
138	|----|---------|
139	| `0` | Success |
140	| `1` | Error |
141	
142	ADR-001 §"Error semantics" declared `rc=1` routes to `kind: recovery` plugins and `rc=2` is fatal. This routing was **never implemented** at the stage-dispatch layer. No recovery plugin has ever been registered. `rc=1` at the stage-dispatch layer has always been a terminal error. The rc table in ADR-001 is superseded.
143	
144	`rc=0` means "my result file is on disk, read it." `rc=1` means "I failed — read my result if present; if it is absent I died, and I am `broken`." **`rc=0` with a missing or unparseable result is a structural failure, not a warning.**
145	
146	Everything anything needs to say beyond those two facts belongs in the result file (§5), not in an exit code.
147	
148	**This binds engine-internal paths too.** The engine currently signals through a private rc vocabulary — `5` blocked, `6` cycle_abort, `8` blocking_member_failure, `9` llm_unavailable, `10` scope_too_large, `11` route_back, `130`/`143` signal. It is a vocabulary that grew one caller at a time, each reader mapping it differently, and it fails the same way the plugin-side table did: `cycle_orchestrator_run` special-cases only `8`, `11` and `130` and collapses every other abort rc to `4` (`config_invalid`), so a `cycle_abort` and a SIGTERM both surface as a configuration error. #1225 fixed that collapse for `11` alone.
149	
150	An integer channel with no declared vocabulary cannot be enforced, which is the defect this whole ADR exists to remove — exempting the engine from its own contract would reproduce it one layer down.
151	
152	So the control flow those codes carry moves onto declared channels: `disposition` (§6) for recoverability, and explicit routing state for the bounded backward edge (ADR-045) and blocking-member halt (ADR-013). Those mechanisms keep working; what changes is that a reader consults a declared field instead of re-interpreting a number. **#1823 owns the narrowing and the designs that re-home each signal**, and its acceptance is the enforcing check: no engine path returns or interprets an rc outside {0,1}, with a guard test enumerating the call sites.
153	
154	#### 4a. Where each signal goes (delivered by #1823)
155	
156	The destination is never new. Every one of these already had a declared channel the engine was setting alongside the number; the re-homing is to *read the word instead of the integer*, which is why `dispatch_rc_legacy_reason` names the vocabulary rather than inventing one.
157	
158	| rc | Re-homes onto | Owner |
159	|----|---------------|-------|
160	| `130`/`143` signal | `interrupted` (§6) — and the ADR-025 `.abort.signal` sentinel, which already carries abort across subshells | #1823 |

162	| rate limit | `unavailable` (§6) since #2111 (was `throttled`, #1823): the run ends, resumable when the limit resets | #1823 / #2111 |

165	| `11` route_back | ADR-045 routing state (`_CYCLE_ROUTE_BACK_*`, `cycle.route_back`). The `route_target` vocabulary is #1767 | ADR-045 / #1767 |

167	| `5` blocked | `_CYCLE_LAST_TERMINATED_REASON ∈ {blocked, no_committed_changes}` + `cycle.blocked` (ADR-021 #528/#1265) | ADR-021 |
168	| `6` cycle_abort | `_CYCLE_LAST_TERMINATED_REASON=cycle_abort` + `cycle.complete reason=` | ADR-021 |

And `_cycle_handle_terminal_rc` had a `130)` arm but no `143)` arm; #1860 merged them into `130|143) reason="aborted"` so SIGTERM and SIGINT agree at the orchestrator fan-in as well as at the dispatch boundary.

175	#### 4b. Coexistence: v1 keeps its rc, v2 is narrowed
176	
177	**(superseded 2026-10-08 by the #1850 amendment below — v1 is refused at load; every stage is narrowed; the inventory is zero)**
178	
179	**The narrowing is gated on `result_contract`, not applied to every plugin at once.**
180	
181	A v1 plugin's exit code is still its *only* channel. `plan` reports `scope_too_large` as rc=10 and has no result field in which to say it; `design`, `validate` and `monitor` all `return 2` for a missing `state_file` per ADR-001 §Runtime. Narrowing every plugin today would delete the meaning of all 25 in a single step, and the engine would keep running past conditions that currently stop it — an oversized scope would no longer abort.

183	So:
184	
185	| Stage speaks | rc | Held to the `disposition` dictionary? |
186	|---|---|---|
187	| `result_contract: 1` (today's 25 plugins) | passes through **unchanged** | No — it declares no disposition, and absence is not an off-set word |

196	### 5. The result file
197	
198	One file. The primary artifact declared in the stage's manifest (`outputs[primary: true]`), read after `run` returns. Mandatory keys:
199	
200	| Key | Meaning |
201	|-----|---------|
202	| `result_contract` | Version of **this contract** the file speaks |
203	| `verdict` | The stage's own word for what happened (§6) |
204	| `disposition` | What the engine should do about it (§6) |
205	| `reason` | Mandatory free text — rendered to logs and terminal, **never branched on** |
206	
207	Plus `data: {}` — open, namespaced, and never interpreted by the engine.
208	
209	`result_contract` is **not** `schema_version`. `schema_version` is the artifact's own schema version and is independent: `build-summary.json` has been at `4` since #602. Conflating the two silently reinterprets every existing artifact.
210	
211	Delivered by #1821 (landed); version negotiation by #1824.
